Scientists capture first images of molecules before and after reaction - they look exactly like the textbook versions!
This. Is. AWESOME. (that's all I've got to say about it, as I almost flunked out of chemistry)
I may have just woken up, but this is definitely coolest thing I've seen all day.
So wait... How did we know they were that shape in the first place?

A lot of more advanced chemistry in recent years has been more about the shape and size of bonds in a molecule, rather than the simple "how much of this do we need to react with that" that early chemistry is about.

As for precisely how we find this stuff out, there are a variety of tools that sort of look at the problem in different ways. For some materials, you can get an idea of how they fit together by looking at the structure of crystals that they form. Another technique is to look at which types of "light" are absorbed and emitted by the material. This is largely determined by the way electrons move in the atomic orbitals and bonds between atoms, so certain wavelengths of radiation tend to correspond with particular structures in the molecule ("groups" in chemistry jargon). The last tool that I'm personally familiar with is nuclear magnetic resonance, which is the same technology that's used in "Magnetic Resonance Imaging" scanners at the hospital. It's just that they put a vial of the chemical in the scanner instead of a person and they don't care about getting an image, just the particular wavelengths that the sample puts out during the scan. (Oh, and the "nuclear" part of the name is left out because very few people want to get stuck in a huge loud scanner even when it's not also "nuclear.")

Of course, these tests haven't really been able to tell us what shape molecules are directly, they're only really good for testing whether a chemist's guess is correct. So chemistry of this type is about a bunch of scientists thinking really hard until they have an idea of what the structure could be based on what they know about how atoms connect and how the chemical responds to more mundane tests, and then they use these advanced techniques to confirm whether that guess is correct or not.
